lessons.title: The Farmer's Puzzle: Why Do Maize and Beans Behave Differently After the Same Rain?

quiz.prompt: Mama Wanjiru in Molo plants maize and beans on the same morning after the first heavy rains. The seeds all look healthy. After one week, which description matches what the story says she found?
choices: All the seeds came up on the same day
Every healthy-looking seed had sprouted
Only the beans came up and every maize seed failed
Some seeds had sprouted, some were late, and a few had not come up at all
quiz.rationale: The story says that after one week some seeds had sprouted, some were late and a few had not come up, even though they looked healthy. This is the puzzle the class will explore.
quiz.placement: Predict: the farmer's story about Mama Wanjiru in Molo

quiz.prompt: While watching a time-lapse of a bean seed growing in soil, four learners wrote notes. Which note is a specific observation, something you can actually see, and not a guess or an explanation?
choices: The bean seed needs warmth to wake up.
Maize and beans grow in exactly the same way.
The bean stem was bent like a hook as it came above the soil.
The plant grew.
quiz.rationale: A specific observation describes something seen, such as the hooked stem. 'The plant grew' is too general, and the other two are explanations or claims, not observations.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'I notice / I wonder' table for the bean and maize time-lapse videos

quiz.prompt: In the time-lapse videos, learners were asked to watch which part of the seedling came out first. Which statement is an 'I wonder' statement rather than an 'I notice' statement?
choices: I notice that the maize leaf was rolled up.
I wonder why some seeds that looked healthy did not sprout.
I notice that some seeds did not sprout.
I notice that the root grew down into the soil.
quiz.rationale: An 'I wonder' statement raises a question about something not yet understood. The other statements describe what can be seen.
quiz.placement: Observe: second viewing of the time-lapse videos, recording 'I notice' and 'I wonder'

quiz.prompt: Your teacher says your first drawn model of a maize seed and a bean seed will not be marked right or wrong, and you will keep it in a folder. What is the main reason for this?
choices: It shows your starting ideas, so you can compare them with your improved ideas at the end of the unit
It will be used to give each learner a final grade for the term
Only learners who draw the correct model are allowed to continue
The teacher already knows that every first model is wrong and will discard them
quiz.rationale: The unmarked Day 1 model is a baseline of honest thinking. Learners return to it at the end of the unit to see how their ideas changed with evidence.
quiz.placement: Explain: drawing and labelling the initial model of a maize seed and a bean seed

quiz.prompt: On Day 1 of the unit, a learner asks: 'Why did some of Mama Wanjiru's healthy-looking seeds not germinate?' Which is the best response at this stage of learning?
choices: Only the biggest seeds germinate, so the small ones failed.
Healthy-looking seeds always germinate, so the farmer must have counted wrongly.
It has not been explained yet, so it goes on the Driving Question Board to investigate with evidence.
Seeds need only water, so the rain should have made every seed germinate.
quiz.rationale: This is the anchor lesson, so the phenomenon is left unexplained. The other choices are the misconceptions 'healthy seeds must germinate', 'seeds need only water' and 'big seeds grow first'.
quiz.placement: Explain: sentence starters 'I think maize and bean plants grow differently because…' and 'I wonder why…'

quiz.prompt: A group wants to post a question on the Driving Question Board about maize and beans. Which question is the best one to investigate?
choices: How does maize grow differently from beans?
Is maize good?
Is Mama Wanjiru a good farmer?
Did it rain in Molo?
quiz.rationale: A good DQB question starts with How, Why or What and can be investigated. The other questions are yes/no or cannot be answered by studying how the plants grow.
quiz.placement: DQB: groups write and improve questions on sticky notes or cards

quiz.prompt: Many groups asked whether growth and development are the same thing. Which question did the class agree to investigate first in the next lesson?
choices: Why is the rainfall heavy in Nakuru County?
What is growth and development?
Which fertiliser is best for maize?
How do plants make their own food?
quiz.rationale: The question that appeared most often when the class sorted the DQB was 'What is growth and development?', so it leads into Lesson 2.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: choosing the first new question from the DQB and the exit ticket link to the driving question

lessons.title: Meaning of Growth and Development; Structure of Monocot and Dicot Seeds

quiz.prompt: A Grade 11 class is discussing how growth differs from development in a maize plant. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
choices: Growth and development mean the same thing, because both describe a plant getting taller.
Growth is a permanent increase in size, dry mass or cell number, while development is a change in form and complexity, such as cell differentiation.
Growth is the formation of new organs such as leaves and flowers, while development is only an increase in height.
Growth is any increase in size, even a temporary one, while development is a decrease in size.
quiz.rationale: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size, dry mass or cell number. Development is the change in form and function, such as differentiation and the formation of leaves, roots and flowers.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on the meaning of 'growth' and 'development'

quiz.prompt: A farmer watches her maize plants over several weeks. Which observation is an example of development rather than only growth?
choices: The maize plant forms a tassel and cobs.
The maize root extends deeper into the soil.
The maize stem becomes taller.
The maize stem becomes thicker.
quiz.rationale: Forming a tassel and cobs is a change in form and function (new organs), which is development. Becoming taller, thicker or longer is a permanent increase in size, which is growth.
quiz.placement: Predict: learners give Kenyan examples of growth and development (end of Think-Pair-Share)

quiz.prompt: A group splits open a soaked bean seed and finds a small embryo between the two cotyledons. Which part of the embryo will grow into the root of the new plant?
choices: The plumule
The radicle
The cotyledon
The testa
quiz.rationale: The radicle is the embryonic root. The plumule becomes the shoot, the cotyledons store food, and the testa is the protective seed coat.
quiz.placement: Observe: identifying the testa, cotyledons, plumule and radicle in the dissected bean seed

quiz.prompt: A learner cuts a soaked maize grain lengthwise and puts a drop of iodine solution on the cut surface. The large whitish area (endosperm) turns blue-black. What does this show?
choices: The endosperm is dead tissue.
The endosperm contains starch, so it is the food store of the maize grain.
The endosperm contains the embryo of the maize grain.
The endosperm has absorbed water, so it will become the root.
quiz.rationale: Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present. The blue-black colour in the endosperm shows that it stores starch as food for the embryo.
quiz.placement: Observe: Step 5, iodine test for food stores on cut surfaces

quiz.prompt: In a maize grain, the coleoptile is a sheath around the plumule. What is its job during germination?
choices: It protects the plumule as it pushes up through the soil.
It absorbs digested food from the endosperm.
It protects the radicle as the root emerges.
It allows water to enter through a small pore.
quiz.rationale: The coleoptile covers the plumule (young shoot) and protects it as it pushes through the soil. The scutellum absorbs digested food, the coleorhiza protects the radicle, and the micropyle lets water in.
quiz.placement: Explain: comparison table of structures and their functions (coleoptile, coleorhiza, scutellum)

quiz.prompt: Which row correctly compares a maize grain (monocot) with a bean seed (dicot)?
choices: Maize: one cotyledon, no food store. Bean: two cotyledons, food stored in the endosperm.
Maize: one cotyledon (scutellum), food stored in the endosperm. Bean: two cotyledons, food stored in the cotyledons.
Maize and bean: two cotyledons, food stored in the endosperm.
Maize: two cotyledons, food stored in the cotyledons. Bean: one cotyledon, food stored in the endosperm.
quiz.rationale: Maize has one cotyledon (the scutellum) and stores starch in a large endosperm. Bean has two fleshy cotyledons that store the food.
quiz.placement: Explain: groups complete the comparison table of monocot (maize) and dicot (bean) seeds and write the Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement

quiz.prompt: A learner draws a model of how a maize grain starts to grow after planting. Which arrow path correctly shows how stored food reaches the embryo?
choices: Endosperm, then the scutellum, then the embryo
Testa, then the embryo
Cotyledons, then the embryo
Coleoptile, then the radicle
quiz.rationale: In maize the food is stored as starch in the endosperm. The scutellum absorbs the digested food and passes it to the embryo. The cotyledon route is for beans, and the testa and coleoptile are protective structures, not food stores.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the Day 1 model by adding arrows showing food moving from the endosperm (maize) or cotyledons (bean) to the embryo

lessons.title: Seed Dormancy: Why Do Some Healthy-Looking Seeds Refuse to Germinate?

quiz.prompt: In Trans Nzoia, a farmer plants maize and beans on the same day after rain. Some healthy-looking seeds never germinate. Which statement best describes seed dormancy?
choices: A state in which the seed has died and cannot grow again
A state in which the seed has no embryo inside it
A resting state in which a living seed does not germinate even when conditions look right
A state in which every seed germinates immediately when watered
quiz.rationale: Dormancy is a resting state of a living seed that does not germinate even when conditions seem suitable. The seed is not dead.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share, introduction of the word 'dormancy'

quiz.prompt: Learners soaked hard-coated Senna seeds in water for several hours. The seeds did not swell. Which is the most likely reason?
choices: The embryo was too large to take up water
The hard seed coat did not let water enter the seed
The seeds had absorbed too much water already
Soaking always kills seeds that have hard coats
quiz.rationale: If a seed does not swell after soaking, water is not entering. A hard, impermeable seed coat blocks water uptake and so keeps the seed dormant.
quiz.placement: Part A: examining seed specimens and comparing dry and soaked seeds

quiz.prompt: In a dormancy-breaking investigation, one container holds untreated seeds kept moist in the same place as the treated seeds. Why is this container needed?
choices: To give the treated seeds extra water
To make sure all the seeds germinate
To show the seeds in the other containers are not dormant
To compare with the treated seeds, so we can tell whether the treatment made a difference
quiz.rationale: The control is untreated but kept under the same conditions. Any difference between it and the treated seeds can then be linked to the treatment.
quiz.placement: Part B: setting up four labelled containers, including the control

quiz.prompt: A group wants to break dormancy in Acacia seeds by scarification. Which action is scarification?
choices: Washing the seeds in several changes of water
Leaving the seeds in dry soil for a month
Rubbing the seed coat lightly on sandpaper or a rough stone
Keeping the seeds in a cool place for some days
quiz.rationale: Scarification means scratching, nicking or rubbing the seed coat so water and gases can enter. Washing is leaching and cool storage is chilling.
quiz.placement: Part B: scarification container (seed coat rubbed on sandpaper or rough stone)

quiz.prompt: A farmer finds that some healthy seeds contain chemical inhibitors that stop germination. Which treatment would best help remove the inhibitors?
choices: Washing the seeds in several changes of water (leaching)
Drying the seeds in the sun for a week
Putting the seeds in boiling water
Rubbing the seed coat on sandpaper only
quiz.rationale: Leaching washes water-soluble inhibitors out of the seed. Sandpaper only opens the coat, and boiling water can kill the embryo.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: causes of dormancy and ways of breaking it

quiz.prompt: After the seed coat of a dormant bean seed is rubbed and the seed is placed in wet cotton wool, the seed swells. What is this uptake of water called, and why is it important for germination?
choices: Imbibition; it activates enzymes in the embryo
Scarification; it makes the seed coat thicker
Leaching; it washes inhibitors out of the embryo
Stratification; it keeps the embryo cold and inactive
quiz.rationale: Water uptake by a seed is called imbibition. It activates enzymes in the embryo so germination can begin.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: reasoning linking water uptake to the embryo

quiz.prompt: Acacia seeds in the Tsavo drylands can stay dormant for a long time. How does dormancy help these plants survive?
choices: It makes the seeds germinate faster than other plants' seeds
It removes the need for water when the seeds finally germinate
It makes every seed in the soil germinate on the first rain
It stops seeds from germinating in a short dry spell, and it spreads germination over time
quiz.rationale: Dormancy lets seeds wait for adequate rain and spreads germination over time. Not all seedlings are then lost to one dry spell.
quiz.placement: Explain: significance of dormancy for plants in Kenyan ecosystems (Acacia in Tsavo)

lessons.title: Germination: Process, Types and Conditions Necessary for Germination in Maize and Bean Seeds

quiz.prompt: A group sets up Container A (moist cotton wool) and Container B (dry cotton wool) to test whether maize and bean seeds need water to germinate. Which of these must be kept the SAME in both containers for the test to be fair?
choices: The type and number of seeds and the temperature
Whether the seeds are alive or boiled
The amount of water given
Whether the cotton wool is wet or dry
quiz.rationale: In a fair test only one variable (water) is changed. The seed type, number of seeds and temperature must stay the same so any difference is caused by water alone.
quiz.placement: Group prediction chart for the 5 set-ups: the variable to change and the ones to keep the same

quiz.prompt: In the germination investigation, one container holds boiled and then cooled maize and bean seeds on moist cotton wool with air and room temperature. Why is this container included?
choices: To show that a seed must be alive (viable) to germinate even when water, air and warmth are present
To show that seeds need cold conditions to germinate
To show that seeds germinate faster when they are boiled
To show that seeds need more water than the control container
quiz.rationale: Boiling kills the embryo. If these seeds fail in good conditions, it shows a viable (living) seed is needed as well as water, oxygen and warmth.
quiz.placement: Part A: Set E, boiled-then-cooled seeds on moist cotton

quiz.prompt: A learner examines two seedlings. In seedling X, the coleoptile and plumule push up while the cotyledon stays below the soil. In seedling Y, the hypocotyl arches and lifts the cotyledons above the soil. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both X and Y are epigeal
X is bean (epigeal) and Y is maize (hypogeal)
Both X and Y are hypogeal
X is maize (hypogeal) and Y is bean (epigeal)
quiz.rationale: Maize shows hypogeal germination, where the cotyledon stays below the soil. Bean shows epigeal germination, where the hypocotyl lifts the cotyledons above the soil.
quiz.placement: Part B: examining germinating maize and bean seedlings and drawing hypogeal and epigeal germination

quiz.prompt: Maize seeds are fully submerged in boiled, cooled water with a thin layer of cooking oil on top. After 5 days, very few have germinated, even though there is plenty of water. What is the best explanation?
choices: The water was too warm for enzymes to work
The seeds had no soil to grow in
The seeds received too much light
Too little oxygen is available for aerobic respiration, so the seeds cannot release the energy needed for germination
quiz.rationale: The oil and boiled water keep oxygen out. Without oxygen, aerobic respiration cannot release energy for germination. This also explains why seeds in waterlogged soil may fail.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: Container C (submerged seeds with oil on top)

quiz.prompt: In a germination test, 9 of 10 bean seeds germinated on moist cotton wool at room temperature with no soil. Which conclusion is supported by this evidence?
choices: Seeds need fertiliser to germinate
Seeds need soil to germinate
Seeds germinate only in the dark
Soil is not necessary for germination if water, oxygen and suitable warmth are present
quiz.rationale: Seeds germinated without any soil, so soil is not a requirement. Water, oxygen and suitable temperature were enough, which corrects the common misconception that soil is essential.
quiz.placement: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning using results from Container A (control)

quiz.prompt: Which list shows the correct order of events in the germination of a maize or bean seed?
choices: Water uptake, enzymes activated, radicle emerges, plumule emerges
Radicle emerges, water uptake, enzymes activated, plumule emerges
Enzymes activated, plumule emerges, water uptake, radicle emerges
Plumule emerges, radicle emerges, water uptake, enzymes activated
quiz.rationale: The seed first takes in water, which activates enzymes. The radicle then breaks out and grows downwards, followed by the plumule.
quiz.placement: Revising the Day 1 model: conditions and labelled diagrams of maize and bean germination

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kitale plants healthy-looking maize seeds after good rain. The soil is moist, well aerated and warm, yet some seeds never germinate. Which is the most likely reason?
choices: The seeds are hypogeal, so they cannot germinate
The seeds did not get enough sunlight underground
The seeds are dead (not viable) or dormant
The soil had too much oxygen
quiz.rationale: When water, oxygen and warmth are suitable, failure points to an internal factor: the seed is dead (non-viable) or still dormant. Seeds do not need light to germinate, and oxygen is needed, not harmful.
quiz.placement: Model revision note: why the farmer's seeds planted together after the same rain germinate at different times or fail

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Growth: How Do Plants Show Growth?

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega watches young maize and bean seedlings after germination. Which parts of each seedling are mainly getting longer?
choices: The whole stem and root grow longer evenly, like an animal growing all over
Only the bark between the xylem and phloem
The tips of the shoot and the tips of the root
Only the old leaves near the soil
quiz.rationale: Growth in length (primary growth) happens at the shoot and root tips, where the apical meristems are. Plants do not grow evenly all over like animals.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on which parts of the seedlings are getting longer

quiz.prompt: A learner views a low-power section of a young bean stem and a young maize stem under a microscope. How are the vascular bundles arranged?
choices: Both stems have bundles in a ring
Bean: scattered through the stem. Maize: in a ring
Bean: in a ring. Maize: scattered through the stem
Both stems have a single bundle in the centre
quiz.rationale: The young dicot (bean) stem has its vascular bundles in a ring, while the monocot (maize) stem has scattered bundles.
quiz.placement: Station 1: prepared slide or photomicrograph of young dicot (bean) and monocot (maize) stems

quiz.prompt: A learner counts 14 rings on a cut Eucalyptus log. What do the rings and the thick trunk show about the tree?
choices: The trunk has grown only in length through primary growth
The trunk has increased in girth through secondary growth
The trunk has thickened by stretching of existing cells only
The trunk has no cambium
quiz.rationale: Annual rings come from new xylem made by the vascular cambium. This is secondary growth, which increases girth.
quiz.placement: Station 2: cut Eucalyptus/Cypress/Grevillea log showing annual rings; count rings and record

quiz.prompt: Bean plants thicken and branch, but maize stems stay mostly the same width. What is the best explanation?
choices: Maize stems have a cambium ring but it is too thin to work
Bean stems thicken only because they take in more water
Maize stems have scattered vascular bundles with no cambium, so they do not thicken much
Maize does not have a shoot tip, so it cannot grow
quiz.rationale: Secondary growth needs a vascular cambium. The bean (dicot) stem has cambium between xylem and phloem. The maize (monocot) stem has scattered bundles and no cambium, so it mostly grows only in length.
quiz.placement: CER: Why do bean plants thicken and branch while maize stems stay mostly the same width?

quiz.prompt: In a 3-step model of secondary growth in a Grevillea stem, the cambium forms a complete ring. What does this ring of cambium produce?
choices: Only cork cells on both sides
New root tips at the base of the stem
Secondary phloem inward and secondary xylem outward
Secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward
quiz.rationale: The vascular cambium makes secondary xylem towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside. This adds to the girth of the stem.
quiz.placement: Build the 3-step model of secondary growth in a woody dicot (Step 2: cambium forms a complete ring)

quiz.prompt: A learner revises a model of maize (hypogeal) and bean (epigeal) seedlings after germination. Which statement should be in the model?
choices: Both seedlings start growing in length by primary growth from the shoot and root apical meristems
Maize grows only by secondary growth, and bean grows only by primary growth
Neither seedling has any meristem
Bean seedlings start with secondary growth, but maize seedlings start with primary growth
quiz.rationale: Both maize and bean begin growth after germination by primary growth at the shoot and root apical meristems. Only the bean (dicot) later adds secondary growth.
quiz.placement: Revise Day 1 model: 'After germination: how the plants grow' with labelled arrows for apical and lateral meristems

quiz.prompt: Which pair correctly matches the type of growth with the meristem and what increases?
choices: Primary growth: lateral meristems, girth increases
Primary growth: apical meristems, length increases
Secondary growth: apical meristems, length increases
Secondary growth: apical meristems, girth increases
quiz.rationale: Primary growth happens at apical meristems and increases length. Secondary growth happens at lateral meristems (vascular cambium and cork cambium) and increases girth.
quiz.placement: End of lesson: teacher mini-explanation and quick quiz on primary and secondary growth

lessons.title: Where Does a Maize or Bean Plant Grow? Measuring Growth and Regions of Growth in Seedlings

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Nakuru plants maize and beans. A student predicts where a young root becomes longer. Which prediction best matches how growth in length happens in a root?
choices: Growth happens only at the part of the root closest to the seed
Growth happens mainly in a region near the root tip, where cells divide and elongate
Growth happens evenly along the whole length of the root
Growth happens only in the oldest part of the root, far from the tip
quiz.rationale: Growth in length is concentrated in the root tip region (apical meristem and the zone of elongation behind it), not evenly along the root.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual drawing and Think-Pair-Share on where growth in length takes place on the seedling

quiz.prompt: Learners mark a young bean root with ink every 5 mm starting from the tip, then return it to moist soil. After 48 hours they measure the distances between the marks. Which marks will have moved furthest apart?
choices: All marks will have moved apart by the same amount
The marks in the oldest part of the root, furthest from the tip
None, because roots only grow in width
The marks nearest the root tip
quiz.rationale: Cells near the root tip divide and elongate, so the spaces between marks there increase most. Marks higher up stay almost the same distance apart.
quiz.placement: Observe: marking maize and bean roots with ink at 5 mm intervals and re-measuring after 24 and 48 hours

quiz.prompt: In the seedling investigation, why do learners mark the root at equal intervals (for example every 5 mm) from the tip?
choices: So that any change in the distance between marks shows which region has grown
So that the ink dries faster on the root
So that the root grows straighter
So that the seedling grows faster
quiz.rationale: Equal starting spacing makes a fair comparison: if one gap becomes larger than the others, growth happened in that region.
quiz.placement: Observe: marking maize and bean roots and shoots at equal intervals, and the teacher question 'Why do we mark at equal distances?'

quiz.prompt: A maize plant was 4 cm tall on day 7 and 32 cm tall on day 21. What was its average growth rate between day 7 and day 21?
choices: 2 cm per day
1.5 cm per day
4 cm per day
28 cm per day
quiz.rationale: Growth = 32 − 4 = 28 cm over 21 − 7 = 14 days. Rate = 28 ÷ 14 = 2 cm per day.
quiz.placement: Observe: plotting the maize and bean growth curves from the height-against-time data table

quiz.prompt: On an S-shaped growth curve of a maize plant (height against time), what does the steep middle part show?
choices: Growth has stopped because the plant is mature
Growth is rapid, with active cell division and photosynthesis
Growth is slowing because resources are limited
The seed is still using stored food and growth is slow
quiz.rationale: The steep part is the rapid (log) phase, when cells divide actively and photosynthesis supports fast increase in height.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER discussion of the S-shaped growth curve and the oral probe 'What does the steep part of the curve show?'

quiz.prompt: A group is writing a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning statement about where a root grows. Which of these is a piece of EVIDENCE?
choices: Growth in length is concentrated at the root tip.
All plants grow in the same way.
This happens because cells in the meristem divide and then elongate.
The marks nearest the root tip moved 8 mm apart in 48 hours, while marks higher up stayed the same distance apart.
quiz.rationale: Evidence is measured data from the investigation. The first choice is a claim, the third is reasoning, and the last is an unsupported statement.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) frame 'I claim that ___. My evidence is ___. This is because ___.'

quiz.prompt: Which statement best defines growth in a plant?
choices: Any change in the shape of the plant, with no change in size
A temporary increase in size caused by a seed absorbing water
An increase in height only
A permanent increase in size and dry mass
quiz.rationale: Growth is a permanent increase in size and dry mass. Swelling from water is temporary, and growth can be measured as height, length, width or dry mass, not height only.
quiz.placement: Explain and DQB: key terms on the board and the misconception 'growth is not only height'

quiz.prompt: Which plant can become thicker through secondary growth, and which tissue is responsible?
choices: Bean, through the vascular cambium
Maize, through the vascular cambium
Maize, through the apical meristem at the shoot tip
Bean, through the apical meristem at the root tip
quiz.rationale: Bean is a dicot and can thicken its stem because of the vascular cambium (a lateral meristem). Maize is a monocot with no secondary growth, and apical meristems cause growth in length.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the poster model of primary growth (apical meristems) and secondary growth (vascular cambium in the bean stem)

lessons.title: Plant Hormones: What Controls Growth in Maize and Bean Seedlings?

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kakamega plants bean seeds on the same day after rain. One healthy-looking seed has not germinated because it is still dormant. Which hormone could help break its dormancy and start germination?
choices: Abscisic acid
Ethylene
Gibberellins
Auxin from the stem tip only
quiz.rationale: Gibberellins break dormancy and promote germination. Abscisic acid maintains dormancy, so it would not start germination.
quiz.placement: Observe: hormone evidence table (video and reading on plant hormones)

quiz.prompt: Which hormone keeps a seed dormant and also causes the stomata of a leaf to close?
choices: Ethylene
Cytokinin
Abscisic acid
Gibberellin
quiz.rationale: Abscisic acid is responsible for dormancy and stomatal closure. Gibberellins do the opposite for dormancy, and cytokinins act in cell division.
quiz.placement: Observe: hormone evidence table, row for abscisic acid

quiz.prompt: Green bananas bought by a trader in Mombasa turn yellow and soft as they ripen. Which plant hormone controls this ripening?
choices: Cytokinin
Gibberellin
Auxin
Ethylene
quiz.rationale: Ethylene is the hormone that stimulates fruit ripening, for example in bananas and mangoes.
quiz.placement: Observe: highlighting an example for each hormone (ethylene: bananas or mangoes sold in Mombasa)

quiz.prompt: A farmer cuts off the tip of a bean stem and soon side shoots start to grow from the lateral buds. What best explains this?
choices: The tip makes abscisic acid that feeds the side buds, so removing it stops branching
The tip absorbs the rainwater, so removing it leaves more water for the side buds
Cutting the tip makes the plant stop making any hormones
The tip makes auxin that suppresses lateral buds, so removing it lets side buds grow
quiz.rationale: This is apical dominance: auxin from the tip suppresses lateral buds. When the tip is removed, auxin falls and lateral buds grow, helped by cytokinins.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER for (C) bean plants that develop side branches while maize stays unbranched, and the teacher's modelled CER on the tip of the bean stem

quiz.prompt: A student writes: 'Hormones are food for the plant, so a plant with more hormones has more energy to grow.' What is wrong with this idea?
choices: Hormones only work on seeds and never on shoots or roots
Nothing is wrong; hormones are the main food of a plant
Hormones are chemical messengers that control growth processes; they are not food
Hormones are found only in animals, not in plants
quiz.rationale: Plant hormones are chemical messengers that coordinate processes such as cell division, elongation and germination. Plants make their own food by photosynthesis.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER rubric oral probes on misconceptions (hormones are food for the plant)

quiz.prompt: Farmers in Kericho root tea cuttings using natural sources such as bulb onion or Aloe extract. Which hormone group do these sources help to supply so that roots form on the cuttings?
choices: Abscisic acid, which keeps the cutting dormant
Ethylene, which ripens the cutting
Gibberellins, which close the stomata
Auxins, which promote the rooting of cuttings
quiz.rationale: Auxins promote root formation on cuttings, which is why natural rooting sources are used in tree nurseries.
quiz.placement: Explain: CER for (D) farmers in Kericho or Nyeri rooting tea or tree cuttings with natural hormone sources

quiz.prompt: Two maize seeds are planted on the same day with the same rain. One germinates in three days and the other takes longer. What is the best explanation that includes hormones?
choices: Hormones respond to conditions such as water, oxygen and temperature, so seeds can differ in when they germinate
Only seeds without hormones can germinate late
Rain alone decides when every seed germinates, so hormones play no part
Hormones replace water, oxygen and temperature, so these factors do not matter
quiz.rationale: Hormones do not replace environmental conditions; they respond to them. Differences in hormone balance, such as gibberellins versus abscisic acid, can change germination time even with the same rain.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the Day 1 model to add hormones and links to dormancy and germination conditions

lessons.title: Measuring Growth: Seedling Height, Stem Width and Growth Curves of Maize and Beans

quiz.prompt: Before measuring anything, a learner predicts that a maize seedling will grow the same number of centimetres every day for 21 days. Which statement about real seedling growth best challenges this prediction?
choices: Growth happens only in the first three days
Growth keeps getting faster every day until the plant dies
Growth is slow at first, then rapid, then slows down and levels off
Growth is steady, so the graph is a straight line
quiz.rationale: Real growth curves are S-shaped, with a lag phase, a rapid phase and a stationary phase, so the growth rate changes over time. A straight line wrongly assumes a constant daily increase.
quiz.placement: Predict: sketching maize and bean height over 21 days (Think-Pair-Share)

quiz.prompt: A group wraps thread once around a bean stem. The thread measures 12 mm against a ruler. Using the method of dividing the circumference by 3, what is the approximate stem width (diameter)?
choices: 12 mm
9 mm
36 mm
4 mm
quiz.rationale: Diameter is about circumference divided by 3, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 mm. 12 mm is the circumference itself, not the width.
quiz.placement: Observe: measuring stem width with thread and ruler

quiz.prompt: A group measures three maize seedlings from the class nursery. Their heights are 30 cm, 32 cm and 40 cm. What is the mean height?
choices: 34 cm
32 cm
102 cm
40 cm
quiz.rationale: Mean = (30 + 32 + 40) ÷ 3 = 102 ÷ 3 = 34 cm. Using several seedlings and finding the mean gives a more reliable value than one seedling.
quiz.placement: Observe: measuring 3 maize and 3 bean seedlings and calculating mean values

quiz.prompt: Mean height data: maize was 8 cm on Day 6 and 48 cm on Day 15. Beans were 3 cm on Day 6 and 17 cm on Day 15. Between Day 6 and Day 15, how many more centimetres did the maize grow than the beans?
choices: 40 cm
14 cm
26 cm
31 cm
quiz.rationale: Maize grew 48 − 8 = 40 cm. Beans grew 17 − 3 = 14 cm. The difference is 40 − 14 = 26 cm, which is evidence that maize grew faster in this period.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing a CER statement using numbers from the table and graph

quiz.prompt: Mean maize height increased from 18 cm on Day 9 to 32 cm on Day 12. It then went from 58 cm on Day 18 to only 62 cm on Day 21. What does the flatter part of the curve between Day 18 and Day 21 show?
choices: The seed has not yet absorbed water
The stationary phase, where growth slows as the plant matures or resources limit it
The rapid phase, where growth is fastest
The plant has died
quiz.rationale: Growth of only 4 cm in 3 days, compared with 14 cm earlier, shows the stationary phase. The plant is still alive, but its growth has slowed.
quiz.placement: Explain: interpreting lag, rapid and stationary phases on the growth curves

quiz.prompt: Maize and bean seedlings were planted on the same day after the same rain. The two growth curves show that growth is not constant, and that the two crops grow at different rates. Why does this lead to the question 'Do we have hormones in plants?'
choices: Because growth speeds up and slows down at different times, suggesting something inside the plant may control its timing and speed
Because seeds that failed to germinate have no growth curve
Because the curves are straight lines
Because plants make insulin like animals do
quiz.rationale: Changing growth rates under the same conditions suggest an internal control. This is what makes learners ask whether plants have hormones as animals do.
quiz.placement: DQB: adding evidence and the new question 'Do we have hormones in plants?'

quiz.prompt: In a revised model of early growth, arrows are drawn showing food stores feeding the young seedling. Which pair correctly shows where maize and bean seedlings get these early food stores?
choices: Maize from the endosperm, beans from the cotyledons
Both from hormones in the soil
Both only from photosynthesis in the first days
Maize from the cotyledons, beans from the endosperm
quiz.rationale: In maize, a monocot, the food is stored mainly in the endosperm. In beans, a dicot, it is stored in the cotyledons. These stores feed early growth before the leaves can make enough food.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the Day 1 drawing with food store arrows, growth curve sketches and a Gallery Walk

lessons.title: Role of Hormones in Plant Growth and Development: Why Do Maize and Bean Plants Grow Differently?

quiz.prompt: A farmer pinches off the very top (the shoot tip) of a young bean seedling. What is the most likely result after two weeks?
choices: More side branches grow because the tip no longer holds back the side buds
The plant dies because the tip is cut off
Nothing changes because plants grow only from water and soil
The plant grows taller than before because it has less to feed
quiz.rationale: The shoot tip makes auxin, which suppresses side buds. When the tip is removed, the side buds are released and the plant branches.
quiz.placement: Predict: Think-Pair-Share on pinching off the tip of a young bean seedling

quiz.prompt: In the dry season, healthy seeds in the soil do not germinate even though they are not dead. Which plant hormone helps to keep these seeds dormant?
choices: Abscisic acid
Cytokinins
Gibberellins
Ethylene
quiz.rationale: Abscisic acid maintains dormancy and stops germination during unfavourable conditions. Gibberellins do the opposite and promote germination.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'Plant Hormones' reading card on abscisic acid and dormancy

quiz.prompt: Two bean seedlings were grown for two weeks. The intact seedling was 30 cm tall with 0 side branches. The seedling with its tip pinched off was 18 cm tall with 4 side branches. Which conclusion is best supported by these results?
choices: Removing the tip kills the plant, so it cannot grow taller
Hormones are found only in animals, so the plants differ by chance
Side branches grow only when a plant is shorter than 20 cm
Removing the shoot tip allowed side buds to grow, so the tip normally suppresses branching
quiz.rationale: The pruned plant is alive and has more side branches, while the intact plant is taller with no branches. This shows the tip controls side bud growth.
quiz.placement: Observe: pruning demonstration of pruned versus intact bean seedlings

quiz.prompt: Traders in Mombasa put green bananas in a closed sack and they ripen faster. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Abscisic acid is released and speeds up the ripening
Ethylene gas given off by the fruit collects in the sack and speeds up ripening
Auxin builds up in the sack and makes the fruit softer
Cytokinins from the sack make the fruit cells divide faster
quiz.rationale: Ethylene is the hormone that ripens fruit. A closed sack traps the gas around the bananas so it has a stronger effect.
quiz.placement: Observe: 'Plant Hormones' reading card on ethylene and ripening bananas and mangoes

quiz.prompt: What does the term 'apical dominance' mean?
choices: The shoot tip bends towards light because of gibberellins
The side buds always grow faster than the main shoot
The shoot tip makes auxin that holds back the growth of side buds
The root tip controls how fast the shoot grows
quiz.rationale: Apical means at the top and dominance means control. Auxin from the shoot tip suppresses the side buds, so the plant keeps a single main stem.
quiz.placement: Explain: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning on hormones and apical dominance

quiz.prompt: Tea farmers in Kericho prune their tea bushes regularly. How does pruning help?
choices: It removes the shoot tips, which reduces apical dominance so side buds grow and the bush becomes bushy
It makes the bush grow taller with one thick stem
It adds abscisic acid to the bush so that it stops growing
It kills the old shoots so that only roots keep growing
quiz.rationale: Cutting off the tips removes the source of auxin that suppresses side buds. The side buds then grow, giving more shoots to pluck.
quiz.placement: Explain: farm applications of pruning tea in Kericho

quiz.prompt: A learner revises their Day 1 model of why maize and bean seeds behave differently. Which addition is correct?
choices: Gibberellins promote germination, but the seed also needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to respond
Hormones alone decide germination, so water and temperature can be removed from the model
Each hormone does only one job, so no arrows should link hormones to each other
Only animals have hormones, so the model should show only seed structure
quiz.rationale: Hormones work together with each other and with the earlier factors such as water, oxygen, temperature and dormancy. Hormones are not the only factor in germination.
quiz.placement: Model: revising the Day 1 model by adding hormone arrows and labels

lessons.title: Synthesis and Application: Explaining the Farmer's Maize and Beans and Planning the Tree Nursery

quiz.prompt: A school in Machakos wants to grow 200 mango and grevillea seedlings from stem cuttings. Which idea would best help the cuttings form roots?
choices: Remove all the leaves and the cut surface so nothing is left to use water
Keep the cuttings in full sun without water so they become strong
Spread fertiliser on the cut end, because fertiliser makes roots form
Apply a plant hormone source such as crushed bulb onion or Aloe gel to the cut end, because auxins stimulate roots to form
quiz.rationale: Auxins stimulate root formation on cuttings, and natural sources such as onion and Aloe can supply rooting substances. Fertiliser does not trigger roots, and cuttings need water and some shade.
quiz.placement: Predict: individual 3-minute prediction on rooting 200 mango and grevillea stem cuttings for a school tree nursery in Machakos

quiz.prompt: In a rooting test, four hibiscus cuttings were treated with crushed bulb onion, Aloe gel, cinnamon powder, or water only. Why is the cutting treated with water only included?
choices: It shows which cutting will die first
It is the best treatment because water is the only thing roots need
It makes sure all the cuttings get the same amount of onion
It is the control, used to compare how many roots form with no rooting substance added
quiz.rationale: The water-only cutting is the control. Comparing it with the treated cuttings shows whether the onion, Aloe or cinnamon caused any change in rooting.
quiz.placement: Observe: Evidence Sorting Station, examining the treated and water-only stem cuttings and the rooting results table

quiz.prompt: A farmer plants healthy-looking bean seeds in warm, moist soil with enough air. Most germinate, but a few do not even after many days. What is the most likely reason for the few that fail?
choices: The seeds are dormant, for example with a hard seed coat, so germination has not been triggered
There is no water in the soil
Beans do not have any hormones
The seeds are monocots, so they cannot germinate
quiz.rationale: Water, air and warmth are present, so the problem lies with the seed. Dormancy, such as a hard seed coat, can stop healthy seeds germinating until it is broken, for example by scarification or soaking.
quiz.placement: Observe: Evidence Sorting Station, sorting seed factors and dormancy-breaking results (soaking, scarification)

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly describes germination in maize and in common bean?
choices: Both are epigeal, because all seeds push their cotyledons above the ground
Maize is hypogeal, with its cotyledon staying underground, while bean is epigeal, with its cotyledons raised above the ground
Both are hypogeal, because seeds always germinate underground
Maize is epigeal and bean is hypogeal, because maize has two cotyledons
quiz.rationale: In maize (monocot) the cotyledon stays below the soil, which is hypogeal germination. In common bean (dicot) the hypocotyl lifts the cotyledons above the soil, which is epigeal germination.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing the CER final explanation (evidence on hypogeal vs epigeal germination)

quiz.prompt: In a class test, 10 soaked bean seeds and 10 dry bean seeds were kept under the same warm conditions. 8 of the soaked seeds germinated and 3 of the dry seeds germinated. What percentage of the soaked seeds germinated?
quiz.rationale: Percentage germination = 8 ÷ 10 × 100 = 80%. This data is evidence that water helps germination because it activates enzymes and hormones that break down stored food.
quiz.placement: Explain: writing the Evidence part of the CER final explanation using class germination data (soaked vs dry beans)

quiz.prompt: A farmer in Kitale plants hybrid maize seeds in dry soil and they fail to germinate. What is the best advice, and why?
choices: Plant the seeds much deeper, because seeds do not need water to germinate
Add hormones to the dry soil, because hormones make seeds grow without water
Use bigger seeds, because only large seeds need water
Plant when the soil is moist, because water activates enzymes and gibberellins that break down stored food for the embryo
quiz.rationale: Water is needed for germination: it softens the seed coat and activates enzymes and gibberellins that digest stored food so the embryo can grow. Hormones cannot replace water.
quiz.placement: Explain: whole-class check with the Kitale farmer's hybrid maize that failed to germinate in dry soil

quiz.prompt: A learner writes: 'Then I thought hormones feed a cutting so it can grow. Now I know...' Which ending is correct?
choices: hormones are food stores in the cotyledons that give the plant energy
hormones are only found in animals, so plants use fertiliser instead
hormones are needed in large amounts, like water, to make plants grow
hormones are chemical messengers made in small amounts that control growth, for example auxins stimulate root formation and apical dominance
quiz.rationale: Plant hormones such as auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid are chemical messengers that regulate growth in small amounts. They are not food, and plants make them.
quiz.placement: Model: 'Then I thought... Now I know... because...' statements comparing the Day 1 model with the final cumulative model
